title: FULL OUTER JOIN, CROSS JOIN, and Self‑Joins 🔄
description: Explore the remaining join types and how to join a table to itself.

slides.title: FULL OUTER JOIN 🌐
slides.content:
# Keep Everything from Both Tables

`FULL OUTER JOIN` returns all rows from both tables, with NULLs where no match exists.

```sql
SELECT c.name, o.order_id
FROM customers c
FULL OUTER JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
```

It includes:
- Customers with orders (matched)
- Customers without orders (NULL order)
- Orders without a customer (NULL customer)

**Note:** SQLite does not support FULL OUTER JOIN directly, but you can simulate with LEFT JOIN + UNION + RIGHT JOIN. We'll focus on standard SQL concepts.

slides.title: FULL JOIN Concept
slides.codeSnippet:
-- Not valid in SQLite, but standard SQL:
SELECT c.name, o.order_id
FROM customers c
FULL OUTER JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;

slides.title: CROSS JOIN 🧮
slides.content:
# Cartesian Product

`CROSS JOIN` pairs every row from the first table with every row from the second. No ON condition.

```sql
SELECT c.name, o.order_id
FROM customers c
CROSS JOIN orders o;
```

If customers has 3 rows and orders 4, the result has 3×4=12 rows. Rarely used intentionally; can be useful for generating combinations.

quizData.question: If table A has 5 rows and table B has 7 rows, how many rows does A CROSS JOIN B return?
quizData.explanation: Cross join produces the Cartesian product: every combination.

slides.title: Self‑Join 🔄
slides.content:
# Joining a Table to Itself

Sometimes you need to compare rows within the same table. For example, find employees and their managers, where both are stored in the same `employees` table.

```sql
SELECT e1.name AS employee, e2.name AS manager
FROM employees e1
JOIN employees e2 ON e1.manager_id = e2.employee_id;
```

Aliases are essential to distinguish the two "copies" of the table.

quizData.question: Why are aliases crucial in a self‑join?

options.text: To distinguish the two instances of the same table

quizData.explanation: Without aliases, you can't refer to columns from different roles of the same table.

slides.title: When to Use Self‑Join 🔍
slides.content:
- Hierarchical data (employees‑managers)
- Sequential data (current vs previous record)
- Finding duplicates within a table

Self‑joins are powerful but can be slow on large tables; indexes help.
